name: Syriac
confidence_why: Nöldeke 1904 and Brockelmann 1912 both describe the Maronite reading as stressing a closed final syllable and otherwise the penult (the Nestorian reading penultimate throughout), and Duval 1881 and Phillips 1866 give compatible weight rules, but Brockelmann 1912, Butts 2013 and Knudsen 2015 hold that the classical language before about 700 had final stress and Lundberg 2025 finds the East Syriac manuscript evidence mixed, so the weight rule is a reading-tradition pronunciation rather than a settled fact about Classical Syriac itself.

catalog_quote: § 56. The Nestorians now put the tone on the penult throughout, and that very distinctly. The Maronites ..., on the other hand, put the tone always, or almost always, on the last syllable, when it is a closed syllable, e. g. ... ozel, ... nezdqef, ... yaumin, ... and so also in endings with a diphthong, e. g. ... talmiddu, ... ebneu. On the other hand they always, or nearly always, put the tone on the penult, when the word ends in a simple vowel : ... eto, ... nite, ... sobe, ... nehwe, ... Occasionally a secondary tone also becomes perceptible. At an earlier time the final syllable invariably had the principal accent. ... I am indebted to my friend Guidi, following the communications made by P. Cardahi, for the data on the accentuation of the Maronites.

new_statements.quote: Grammarians have given a few rules for placing the Accent. 1. In words of two syllables, if the first syllable terminate in a consonant without a vowel, this syllable has the accent; as, rám-sho, evening; gármo, bone. 2. If on the contrary the final letter of the word be without a vowel, then the accent is put on the second syllable; as, i-léd, he begat; po-kéd, commanding. If each syllable be formed in that manner, still the second is affected with the accent; as, pek-dáth, she has visited. [...] 3. In words consisting of more than two syllables, the accent is generally placed on the penultimate; as, po-rách-to, bird; me-khúl-to, meat; mart-yo-nu-tho, admonition.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Syriac has an empty rule field and there are no existing stress statements, so Phillips supplies the first placement statement: penult by default, final when the final syllable is closed (disyllables) or the word ends in -o. Nothing in the catalog to agree or conflict with.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent falls on the penultimate syllable by default (rule 1 for disyllables with a closed first syllable; rule 3 'generally' for all words of three or more syllables), but in disyllables a closed final syllable (final consonant without a vowel) draws the accent onto the final syllable even when the first syllable is also closed (i-léd, po-kéd, pek-dáth). All the polysyllabic examples have an open final syllable, so the pattern is: closed ultima stressed, otherwise penult.
new_statements.exceptions: Nouns ending in -o (the -u/-o suffix written with waw) take the accent on the second (final) syllable even without a closed ultima; rule 3 is hedged with 'generally'. The Syriac-script example omitted at '[..]' is a noun ending in o. Phillips attributes the rules to 'Grammarians', i.e. the traditional reading pronunciation, not to his own observation.
new_statements.identity_note: Phillips's examples are in Serto script with West Syriac vocalisation (zqapha rendered 'o': gármo, po-rách-to, me-khúl-to), so his accent rules describe the West Syriac (Maronite/Jacobite) reading tradition of Classical Syriac, not East Syriac and not the reconstructed classical-period pronunciation.

readall_conflicts: Only one listed work (Phillips 1866) was in scope and it was opened; within it there is no internal disagreement. For context, the three Syriac sources already held by the project in the same check folder from the 2026-09-16 pass differ from Phillips by period and reading tradition rather than by data: Brockelmann 1912 (Syrische Grammatik, 3rd ed., §§35-37) says that in the classical period the old free accent had been wholly displaced by ultimate stress ('der alte freie Accent ganz durch die Ultimabetonung verdrängt'), with a secondary accent on the penult, and that only around 700 CE did the main accent begin to shift to the penult, first before an open ultima, a stage the Maronites preserve while the Nestorians carried the penult shift through completely; Lundberg 2025 (in the Khan Festschrift, OBP 0463, pp. 821-822) reports Nöldeke's account (East Syriac distinctly penultimate; Maronites ultimate if closed, penultimate if the ultima is open), Duval's penultimate view, and Knudsen 2015's conclusion that ultimate stress was in the dominant set Late Classical Syriac. Phillips's rules (closed ultima stressed, otherwise penult) coincide with the Maronite/West Syriac reading tradition as Nöldeke and Brockelmann describe it, so they describe a later reading pronunciation, not the reconstructed classical-period ultimate stress. A catalog entry should therefore state which stage or tradition it records; 'weight-sensitive (closed ultima, else penult)' is the reading-tradition valu…

If reading traditions are the object, keep weight-hedged but label it explicitly 'West Syriac (Maronite) reading tradition, second-hand (Guidi/Cardahi), hedged'.

sources.citation: Butts, Aaron Michael. 2013. Language Change in the Wake of Empire: Syriac in its Greco-Roman Context. PhD dissertation, University of Chicago (already held under our earlier reading; re-read now).
sources.quote: 'In Syriac, accent is related to word stress and falls almost always on the last syllable.' fn. 219: 'There are only a few exceptions, such as the imperatives, e.g., qṭulayn(y) "kill me!".' States fixed-final stress for the classical language (agrees with Brockelmann §35, Knudsen 2015:171 and Nöldeke §56's last sentence), not the Maronite weight rule our 'kind' encodes.

sources.citation: Brockelmann, Carl. 1912. Syrische Grammatik mit Paradigmen, Literatur, Chrestomathie und Glossar. 3. Aufl. Berlin: Reuther & Reichard (archive.org syrischegrammati00brocuoft; Glottolog lists the 1905 ed.).
sources.quote: §35: the old free accent was 'ganz durch die Ultimabetonung verdrängt worden, die während der klassischen Periode der syr. Literatur die herrschende blieb.' §36: secondary accent on the penult in many words. §37: 'Erst gegen Ende der klassischen Periode um 700 begann ... eine Verschiebung des Hauptaccents auf die Paenultima, zunächst bei offener Ultima. Diese Betonung haben die Maroniten noch erhalten ... Bei den Nestorianern ist dagegen die Accentverschiebung auf die Paenultima jetzt ganz durchgeführt.' Confirms both tradition statements in our record and dates the Maronite open-ultima/penult

sources.citation: Duval, Rubens. 1881. Traité de grammaire syriaque. Paris: F. Vieweg (archive.org traitedegrammair00duva).
sources.quote: §156: native grammarians (Barhebraeus) give no information on stress; following Stoddard's Neo-Syriac grammar (penult almost always) Duval assumes the same for ancient Syriac. §157: 'l'antépénultième n'a jamais le ton, l'ultième ne le reçoit, en dehors des monosyllabes ... que lorsqu'elle est close par une consonne et renferme une voyelle forte (longue à l'origine)'; otherwise penult; future preformatives stressed (néqtol). An inductive reconstruction, weight-sensitive (final superheavy CVVC), broadly in line with the Maronite-type rule but requiring a long vowel; Lundberg 2025:822 summarises
